22. It is true that in law a conviction for an offence does not necessarily depend upon the corpus delicti being found, there may be reliable evidence, direct or circumstantial of the commission of murder though corpus delicti is not traceable. In the instant case there is absolutely no direct evidence of witnesses except the confessional statements of the alleged murderer which is also subjected to criticism and the story of murder given in the confession appears to be hard to believe and, therefore, it is necessary to pose a question as to whether the corpus delicti is found or not in the instant case. It appears that the police remained satisfied with the skeleton which was recovered from the Bhedagari beel but did not make any effort for its proper identification and to record it in the inquest report. From the condition of corpus delicti which was admittedly decomposed with the skeleton as its remains, it was probably not possible for anyone to identify it, and the evidence of some witnesses suggests so. Under such circumstances it is not understood as to how it could be said by the police or by anybody that it was the dead body of a female and for that matter it was the skeleton dead body of Shahida. The doctor has also failed to perform his duty properly as required under the medical jurisprudence referred to by the learned Advocate for the appellants. Modi's Text Book on Medical Jurisprudence and Toxicology (20th Edition at page 80) sets down certain principles in question and answer forms to be applied for ascertainment whether it was a corpus of a human being and if so whether it is of a male or female and also for ascertaining the age of the person whose skeleton was produce before the doctor. The doctor depended on the guess work of the constable who escorted the dead body but he has not done the ossification of bones and taken recourse to chemical analysis and other methods suggested in the medical jurisprudence for ascertaining the age of the deceased. In the inquest report PWI admitted that it could not be mentioned whether the skeleton is of Shahida. PW 3 Md. Sher Ali admitted that it is not stated in the challan as to whose skeleton it was, PW13 Md. Azizur Rahman stated that it is not written in the inquest report that it was the corpus delicti of a female. Thus the question arises as to whether the skeleton found was the skeleton of Shahida in the absence of which death could not be proved and in case the death is not proved the involvement of the accused appellant becomes a far fetched phenomenon. In the absence of proof that the skeleton recovered was that of Shahida added with the evidence of PW 4 Khalilur Rahman to the effect that the Chhutipur graveyard is situated at one side of the Bhedagari bed and on the other side of the heel situates Baliapur village and that there is a cremation ground nearby and sometimes the dead bodies are left there without cremating them, the prosecution case becomes more doubtful. The recovery of the skeleton without any proof as to whose skeleton it was does not lead us to the irresistible conclusion that it was the skeleton of Shahida. The State reported in PLD 1969 (Dhaka) page 504 relevant 513. In those cases and also in the case of Safar Ali and others Vs. The State reported in 36 DLR for the prolonged custody of the accused persons in the police station before production to the Magistrate it was held that the confessions of the accused were not voluntary. The learned Advocate has also referred to the case of Habibur Rahman alias Habib Vs. The State reported in BCR 1986 (HCD) 278 where the confession was found to be not voluntary as the time for reflection was not given by the Magistrate before recording confession. In the instant case also we find from the prescribed form for recording statement that there is nothing mentioned as to how such time was given to the accused for reflection. In support of the contention that the accused persons before making the confession is required to be questioned by the learned Magistrate for ascertaining the fact whether the confession is voluntary or not the learned Advocate has cited the case of Abdul Wahab and another Vs. State reported in 1988 BLD 344 the case of Nurul Hoque and others Vs. the State reported in 20 DLR 780 and the case of Harbar Singh Bhan Singh Vs. State of Panjab reported in AIR 1957 (SC) 637. It is found in the case of Hamzo Vs. The State reported in 1960 PLD (Karachi) 817, that a person before the confession was recorded had been detained by the police for 2 days but having obtained a remand and no attempt was made by the prosecution to explain the illegal detention by the police and it was held that the confession had the appearance of having been improperly obtained. In the case of State Vs. Ratan Shikder reported in 1969 PLD (Dhaka) 500 it is held that the accused making confession a few months after the occurrence showing him as seriously injured and subsequently retracted it will not be safe to hold it as voluntary.
